title: Wave 14 - Piano arrangements by a model, accepted by machine (promoted from rnd)
verifier_note: Promoted from the rnd bench entry 2026-10-08-llm-piano-arrangement-from-a-generated-brief, whose six claims were all marked verified. lanes.title: Music is a seconds grid, not a prompt

findings.title: Piano arrangements written in LilyPond by a reasoning model and accepted by machine gates
findings.finding: Kimi-K3 (moonshotai/kimi-k3 on OpenRouter, temperature 0, reasoning effort high) wrote complete solo-piano arrangements of Amazing Grace and America the Beautiful in LilyPond: an introduction, one pass per stanza with a texture that builds from verse to verse, and a coda. Three machine gates decided acceptance: LilyPond 2.24 compiles the file with no error or warning; a MIDI import finds every verse's melody in the piano at its written time; and the score clock refuses any sung note with no piano note under it. Both arrangements passed all three (one after a recorded one-line fix), and the Director approved both recordings by ear on 2026-10-08.
findings.implication: A model can write the accompaniment as code, but the gates accept it, not the model. Put rules in the brief that a machine can check (the melody as the top voice at its written time in every pass; no \partial after the start; no pedal marks, repeats, tuplets or \ottava), so a failure is a measured miss rather than a matter of taste. Keep the brief, the system prompt, the raw answer, the compiled .ly and a meta.json (sha256 of each, generation id, usage, cost, any hand fix) per arrangement.

findings.title: A brief generated from the hymn data rather than written by hand
findings.finding: scripts/arrange-hymn.ts builds the brief from the hymn's own data: the melody bar by bar in LilyPond absolute pitches with chords per beat, every stanza, the form (introduction, one pass per stanza, coda), a texture plan, and the checkable rules. America the Beautiful's brief was generated this way, and its answer compiled as returned. Amazing Grace's brief was written by hand before the script existed: it asked for a \partial 4 at the start, so its MIDI import needed an offset of 768 ticks, and its answer needed the one hand fix. The comparison is one generated brief against one hand-written brief.
findings.implication: Generate the brief from the same data the score clock reads, so the model is told exactly what the gates will check. With one arrangement each way, treat 'a generated brief compiles cleaner' as directional until more hymns go through the script.

sources.claim: The script that generates the brief from the hymn data and gates the answer.
brief_note: written by hand before arrange-hymn.ts; \partial 4; import offset 768 ticks.

findings.title: What an arrangement costs: output tokens, most of them reasoning
findings.finding: Amazing Grace: 1,728 prompt tokens and 19,510 completion tokens, 13,023 of them reasoning; $0.298; 196 s. America the Beautiful: 1,956 prompt tokens and 67,147 completion tokens, 36,692 of them reasoning; $1.013; 528 s. Both calls were served by the provider Modal and billed at $3.00 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Completion tokens were over 98% of each bill, and reasoning was 55-67% of the completion. With max_tokens at 200,000 the worst case is about $3.00; the script prints that estimate and spends only when run with --yes.
findings.implication: Budget an arrangement as max_tokens times the output price; the brief costs under a cent. A longer hymn costs more in reasoning, not in input. Record the usage block from the provider in meta.json, because the per-token price depends on which provider serves the call.

findings.title: Small syntax slips: two of three model-written arrangements needed a one-line fix
findings.finding: Of the three hymn arrangements the studio has had a model write, two needed a one-line fix before LilyPond 2.24 would compile them. Amazing Grace wrote \key g major without the backslash before the mode, twice. The Battle Hymn (arranged on 2026-09-26 by an earlier route, before arrange-hymn.ts) left out \language "english". America the Beautiful compiled as returned. Each fix is written into the arrangement's record.
findings.implication: Expect small syntax slips even when the music is right. The compile gate catches them, and a recorded one-line fix is cheaper than a second call. Keep the fix in meta.json, so the published file and the model's answer differ only by what is written down.

sources.claim: rnd entry: the Battle Hymn's missing \language "english", checked 2026-10-08.

findings.title: Rights: model and provider terms that leave a hymn arrangement free to dedicate CC0
findings.finding: The Kimi K3 License grants and conditions the Software (the weights, code and documentation) and asserts no ownership of the model's outputs; its display requirement (section 3) applies only to large commercial products built on the model. OpenRouter's Terms take only a non-exclusive licence in content passed through the service (sections 5.8, 6.1 and 6.2). The hymns' tunes and texts are in the public domain: every edition followed dates from 1919 or earlier, every author died before 1930, and each brief carries the hymn's own melody and chords, not a modern harmonisation. The studio dedicated both arrangements CC0.
findings.implication: A model-written arrangement of a public-domain hymn can ship CC0 when the model licence claims no rights in outputs, the provider's licence in content is non-exclusive, and the brief carries only public-domain material. Check all three for each model and each hymn, because terms change. This records what the terms say; it is not legal advice.

sources.claim: Kimi K3 License: the grant covers the Software; no clause claims the outputs.
OpenRouter Terms sections 5.8, 6.1, 6.2: a non-exclusive licence in content.

lanes.licence_notes: The arrangements are dedicated CC0 by the studio (finding 5). The receipts cited are in public studio repositories. The Kimi K3 License and OpenRouter Terms are cited, not reproduced.
lanes.gaps: Two arrangements by one model through one script. No comparison across models, no second hymn through a generated brief, and no listener test beyond the Director's approval. Whether a generated brief reduces hand fixes is one pair, not a rate.
